did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with the declaration, “The LORD reigns,” and immediately describes a response that encompasses the whole world: the earth and the many islands are called to rejoice. From the very beginning, the LORD’s rule over all the earth is emphasized.

Clouds and thick darkness surround the LORD, yet the foundation of his throne is not mysterious: “righteousness and justice.” The verse connects a transcendent revelation with a reign founded on justice and righteousness.
Fire is described as going before the LORD and consuming his enemies all around. This is a powerful image of a divine presence that does not remain hidden, but acts and inspires awe.
His lightning lights up the whole world, and the earth trembles in response. The chapter’s description of nature emphasizes that this revelation is not merely local, but is felt throughout the world.
The mountains of the world are compared to wax melting before the LORD. The image portrays even mountains—symbols of stability and strength—as unable to stand before the Lord of all the earth.
The heavens themselves are described as proclaiming the LORD’s righteousness, while all the nations see his glory. In this verse, creation and humanity together acknowledge the LORD’s reign.

Those who worship idols and boast in false gods are called to be ashamed, and the verse concludes: “Worship him, all you gods.” The contrast is between idolatry and recognition of the LORD’s supremacy.

The joy of Zion and the towns of Judah is explicitly connected to the LORD’s judgments. They rejoice not merely because of a victory, but because divine justice and righteousness are being established in the world.

The verse emphasizes the LORD’s supremacy through three cumulative expressions: he is Most High over all the earth, exalted far above all, and above every “god.” Thus, the song reinforces the exclusivity and supremacy of his reign.

The final part of the psalm contains a practical appeal: those who love the LORD are called to hate evil. Alongside this moral duty comes a promise of protection for the faithful, while light and joy are described as belonging to the righteous and upright in heart. The ending therefore calls them to rejoice in the LORD and give thanks for his holiness.
